title: Call: Ahmed Zia, Capital A and Jason Mudd, Axia Public Relations

sentences.text: Hello.
Hi, Jason.
How are you doing?
I'm well.
How are you, Andrew?
Yeah, not too bad, thank you, not too bad.
Whereabouts are you calling from today?
I live Amelia Island, Florida, which is north of Jacksonville on the Atlantic Ocean.
Nice.
Wow, what a beautiful place to live.
Fantastic.
Yeah, I love it here.
Yeah.
Have you been there for a while or is, is that where you're from?
Yeah, it's kind of where I'm from.
So I, I'm very fortunate to, you know, have found this place through, I guess just my, my folks moving here when I was young.
Yeah.
Wow, that is lucky.
That's where everybody's moving now anyway, so.
It is, it is.
In fact, we're very fortunate.
We moved here about 20 years ago.
Or else we wouldn't probably be able.
To afford it anymore.
I see.
Yeah, I'm sure it's getting expensive.
I know a few New Yorkers have moved, moved that way and some Californians as well.
So.
Yeah, it's definitely, definitely a load of people moving in.
Yeah.
We joke that people have moved here for what we have, but have wanted to bring their politics with them.
So trying to keep everything well balanced here.
Right.
So.
Yeah.
Wow.
Definitely.
There's a lot of liberals moving in, if that's what you mean.
Yeah.
Just meaning that people like what we have here, so they want to move here, but then they're like, well, why don't we do this and why don't we do that?
And a perfect example is this used to be a real quiet town and you know, people didn't honk their horns and now, you know, right before the light turns red, people try to honk their horns.
I'm like, we don't do that here.
You know, like, what do you, what, you know, you need to lose that habit.
So it's just stuff like that where it's like, you know, we're, I guess just a little bit more laid back and, and considerate and if you're in a hurry, this is the wrong place to be.
It sounds like New Yorkers to me.
Yeah, exactly, exactly.
My sister in law lives in South Carolina.

She moved there from up north somewhere, but she said that there's tons of New Yorkers moving there because of the, the timeline, the time zone and just trying to get out of the city for a quieter life.
But yeah, they're bringing, they bring their stress with them, so.
Yeah, that's right.
The fact they want to live in.
A small town, they want the small, you know, slower pace, but then they can't get out of Their own way sometimes.
Yeah, exactly.
Well, thank you for getting on the call today.
I know we, we booked in with you, but obviously we're in the process here of listing and selling our client, Lesley Francis, pr so keen to sort of move the ball down the field today if possible.
And I'll just kind of take you through who we are and what next steps are that we're looking for.
We're capital A, we're an M and A advisory for marketing services companies.

So all of our clients are either sell side clients, agency owners looking to exit, and we work on the buy side as well, working with financial buyers and agency owners as well who are looking to expand through making acquisitions.
So we get to see a lot of deals because we're on the buy side and the sell side we know what a good deal looks like as well.
So obviously great for our sell side clients who are looking for an exit.
And in this instance with Lesley Frances, pr, we have a client who is eventually looking at a retirement sale.
It isn't a retirement sale today, but she's in her 50s and she's looking to take her foot off the gas at some point in the future.
So she's looking to become part of a bigger group.
You know, she's hoping that she will have some kind of legacy and her staff will be looked after going forward, but she, for now looking to be part of a bigger company before she does that.
And so it's kind of like a two phased sort of move that she wants to make.
And our role in this really is to find that larger company.
And it looks like you guys could be a really good fit.
And I know you've requested some financials first because you have a board meeting coming up, but just to get clear on our process.
So we don't like release financial information in depth from the data room until we are at the next steps, which is when we're looking to get an LOI or an offer from a potential buyer.
And I think we're still kind of a little bit early on that.
So I'm just looking to get a clearer picture on where you are and what your process is.

Because normally our next step now would be to introduce you to our buyer, see if there's some chemistry and if there's a good fit on both sides, then obviously we can invest more time and energy into releasing that financial data.
So how does that sound?
Does that make sense?
Yeah, I appreciate your process.
We're simply just trying to figure out, you know, what size clients she works with to make sure that we're not, you know, acquiring a book of business.
That would be the smallest book of business that we have.
You know, and I know the market she's located in and the way the clients sound, you know, we're guessing they probably are smaller in nature.
And so we just want to make sure we're acquiring something we see as valuable.
So we have that information in one of the slides in the deck.
So in there, it does have the list of revenue by client breakdown.
So it gives you the percentage of the overall revenue the client represents.
So you would be able to get a real steer from that as to what the size of the clients are.
You know, just as a.
As a quick sort of finger in the wind.
You're roughly looking 10% for two of the clients.
Each one's 12 and a half percent, one's nearly 9%.
So, you know, given the revenues in the business of around 600,000.
So there's larger clients around 60,000 each a year.
So is that the kind of size that you're looking for, or does it represent clients that are too small?
Yeah, I don't.

I don't know for sure, but I would just say that, you know, we're interested in seeing how many clients are going to be, you know, around 5,000, 5,500amonth and more, because that's our smallest account right now that we have at our agency.
Yeah.
So, I mean, she's got a big chunk of clients that are also around the 5% of revenue mark.
So that would be around sort of 20, 25, 20, $25,000 a year.
I know you're talking about 5,000 per month.
Is that or on retainers or is that something else?
Yeah.
So our.
Right now, the smallest client we take on is about 5,500amonth in adjusted gross income.
And it's, you know, what we would call like a permanent program client as opposed to, like, project clients.
So generally speaking, we don't.
We don't take on project work unless it's from an existing client.
And we're definitely not looking to acquire a company that is heavily invested in doing mostly project work.
Right.
Okay.
So.
So these are.
There's retained clients here.
And are you able to access the im.
Ahmed, have we shared the.
The.
I am already with Jason.
Yeah.
Just in case you do have access to it.
You should have access.
Yeah, I think so.
I think you sent me the slides.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So, I mean, it was.
It was a really nice presentation.
Oh, thank you.
So the.
The 18th slide slide 18 has, like, the breakdown of revenue by clients.
So you can see she does have a big chunk between 2 and a half percent and 5% where the majority of her clients sit.
And they would, I guess, represent probably half the size of what you're talking about.
It would be around the $30,000 a year mark for a big chunk of those clients.
Right?
Yeah.
Okay.
Too small.
I mean, there are obviously clients around the.
The mark that you're talking about as well, around 50, $60,000 a year.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Okay.
Yeah, that's.
That's kind of what I was thinking as well, but I didn't want to make any assumptions.
But those.
Yeah, those do sound a little bit more on the lower end of what we're looking for.
Right.
Okay, well, so.
So next steps for us, and I'm sure you can see why it would save us a hell of a lot of time and privacy for our clients.
Sharing too much information up front.
You know, the next steps for us would really.
To get you.
Get you both in the room or a zoom, should I say, you know, to have a.
A good chat about what it is that you're trying to achieve and whether that's something that they can buy into.
And there's a chemistry between the two firms.
So that's what we would be looking for next.
If it sounds like the company is too much on the small side, then obviously we can pause it for now if it's not going to be a fit for your investment strategy.
Yeah, yeah, I think our investment strategy.
Is one of which, you know, if.
We'Re going to acquire accounts, we want to make sure they're well targeted for.
What we're looking for.
And I was really hoping that this might, you know, turn out to be that way.
But based on what you're sharing, I'm not sure that it's going to be for us.
Right.
Okay.

All right, well, why don't we get a little bit clearer about what it is that you are looking for, and then we can definitely help you going forward, either referring other clients that we have that might be a good fit, or we are obviously speaking to a lot of target agencies, around 100 new agencies every month between myself and my team.
So it's likely that we'll come across some potential agency businesses to refer to you in the future.
So what is it that you're looking for?
It's priority PR companies.
Is there any particular vertical that you're looking in.
Right now?
Our two primary verticals are going to be home improvement and family entertainment.
Centers, especially those that offer franchise opportunities.
But, you know, we've got a fairly.
General client base right now, and we're not opposed to, you know, acquiring, you know, companies that, that, that have, you know, a broader, you know, niche vertical.
Right, okay, so it could be broader.
And then in terms of like geography and size, is there any considerations there?
Not necessarily, you know, as long as it makes sense.
So, you know, we don't want to do is acquire a company to get lower margin accounts than what we have today organically.
And that's probably one of our primary things.
So, you know, currently we don't, as I mentioned earlier, we don't offer products to, you know, new clients.
We'll take projects from existing clients that are already under some kind of retainer, that are long term, you know, type clients.
Our average client right now is around 12,000amonth, and our smallest is around 55 or is 5,500amonth.
So we would be looking for kind of a makeup that looks more like that.
Okay, so 12k a month and they're retained.
And all these numbers I'm throwing out are adjusted gross income.
So after any outside cost to service the client, we don't have a lot.
Of that because we don't do a.
Lot of paid media.
But, you know, we're looking at those numbers after, you know, our just various cost of goods sold.
Okay, so that's this gross profit you're talking about.
Yeah, I'm told that's not the exact same terminology, but I think it's okay.
Yeah, no, it's similar.
So a lot of agencies do what you're saying.
There's a, there's like an overhead that's attached directly to the client's costs.
So if it goes through the business, it becomes a little bit more of a gray area, doesn't it?
But yeah, it kind of is almost a gross profit margin.
Okay, and then in terms of like the services that you're looking for.
So is there anything in particular?
Because obviously this one business does web development, social media content.
Are you looking for something that's similar or is it more closely aligned to what you're offering with the PR services?
Yeah, we offer the same scope of services, so news content, social content, web content.
So we're very similar in that regard.
Okay, all right.
Yeah, there's plenty of those types of businesses around.
And then in terms of the actual size of the transaction you're looking to do is, I mean, because this is a fairly small one, so is.
Right.
Digestible size that you're Looking to do?
Yeah, perhaps.
I think the challenge is that a.
Company of that size is.
You know, how do you say, not going to.
Have a lot of ideal clients of our size.
So I think that's part of the challenge for us as we look at this and other acquisition targets is how do we make, how do we make that make sense, you know, for our business?
So I mean, if you don't mind me asking, roughly whereabouts are you guys in terms of like ballpark revenue?
Are you doing tens of millions or you're on the 5 million mark?
We're around 5 million of AGI and yeah.

And so, you know, what we're really looking at is, you know, acquisition of a counts and then, you know, maybe talent, we've got, you know, good talent in certain areas, but maybe not and, and others.

So one thing that could be sorry for the wind, one thing that could be attractive to us is acquiring other digital marketing agencies because we have, you know, the PR that we can bolt on and add to those clients and they've got clients that, you know, already getting digital services.
So we've been really intentional about growing our percentage of AGI billings among social media and web content.
And we've got that right about where we want it to be almost.

And so one thing that would be interesting to us is acquiring more digital marketing type agencies, more content agencies, so that we can not only bring our, you know, news capability and traditional PR capabilities such as, you know, getting them thought leadership, positioning and speaking engagements and awards, but, but also, you know, just kind of leveraging that the talent of the agency we might acquire in that regard.
Okay, cool.
And then what are you looking to do to fund the acquisition?
Do you have like a war chest or are you looking to take on some debt?
What's your options?

Yeah, my thought, I definitely don't have a war chest, but definitely, you know, looking into the options that exist depending on the acquisition and the cash flow of the, of the target that we're looking to acquire.
You know, they could be, you know, if they're obviously profitable, you know, we could take the profits and use those to make the, any loan payment.
You know, we've had some opportunities where it would be potentially seller financed and you know, have other options to bring capital to the table.
So.
Okay, cool.
All right, so like an SBA loan or something along those lines, if it was suitable in terms of the size and the profitability.
Okay, cool.
All right, so I think in this instance, particularly as it sounds like these smaller deals you're looking to Kind of just take the book of business rather than continue to run the agency.

It might not be a great fit, but we will go back and double check just to see whether there is, you know, sort of more of these deals that you're looking for, the size that you look for, the sort of 5k month minimum.
And we'll just look into that and confirm for you if it is a majority share of the business that is that then it still might be a suitable deal for you today.
Yeah, yeah, I would.
I mean, honestly going into it I was a little skeptical about, you know, those size deals being available with this.
Particular firm and mostly because the market.
They'Re in and then the types of clients that they, you know, show that they work with just seem to be, you know, pretty small businesses.
Yeah, it is, it's a small local business.
Yeah, but we can double check that.
Yeah, I didn't want to make any.
Assumptions there, but yeah.
And then when, you know, when it.
Comes to acquiring, you know, we are.

Very, I mean to us it's challenging to buy these service based companies because you know, you don't know how long the clients are willing to stick around and you don't know how happy they are from the beginning kind of thing.
And then, you know, and then we just have to assess the talent and the clientele, you know, on a case by case basis.

So, you know, generally speaking, most of the opportunities I've looked at the owner is wanting to leave, you know, promptly and you know, it just depends as you know, whether or not they've developed the talent internally to stay on board and be a value to the, to the clients in the agency or if it's, you know, mostly owner ran with some, you know, assistance serving in various, you know, titles.
So yeah, you know, but for us it's just, you know, the, the, the, how do you say.
That's why I wasn't ready to meet the owner because I just want to know more about the makeup of the accounts because that's ultimately what we're acquiring is the accounts.
I don't see any talent at this agency that's, you know, must have or that stands out with, you know, sophisticated experience or, or our background kind of thing.
So that's what I was looking at to see if it made sense.
Yeah, you know, from an account standpoint.
I mean, Leslie herself, like I said, so she's not looking to leave immediately.
She would prefer to be part of a larger business.
She's actually extremely talented PR person.
She's built a multi million pound business before in the uk she's actually.
Yeah, from the uk.
So she sold a large business before and exited a large business previously.
She is quite experienced herself.
Yeah, no, I saw that.
I just, I was in the impression that she wasn't looking to stick around.
She's not looking to leave immediately.
Okay.
I mean, she, she is getting older, so it's a consideration in the future, but it's not, it's not an immediate thing.
Yeah.
Okay.
Okay.
Well, let me talk to Leslie and see whether this would be something that she could stomach.
Because my feeling is that she, she's not looking to sort of have the, the business broken up and just have the business, the book of business taken out.
Yeah, she, she wants to join a small regional or a larger but regional firm so that she can be part of it.
All right, cool.
Yeah, thanks, Jason.
Look, we're definitely going to keep our eyes out for anything else that's a good fit.
So it's worth checking back with us every so often.
If you're on our mailing list, for sure, when we list agencies, you'll.
You'll get an alert about that as well.
Yeah, that sounds great.
I, I wasn't on your list.
I hope I am now.
My friend Jordan sent me it, sent it to me because, you know, he's on your list, I guess, and he said that this might be a good opportunity for us.
And, you know, I looked into it, but yeah, I mean, my gut tells me this probably isn't a good fit for what Leslie wants and what we want in this particular case.
But ultimately I'm just glad to have, you know, the opportunity and the connection today.
And, yeah, you know, we'll see if something comes along to meet our, you know, unique criteria.
Yeah, I think it will.
You know, there's a lot of businesses coming onto the market the last month or so, so I should imagine there'll be something else getting listed pretty quickly.
And if not, I mean, we do actually work on the buy side as well, doing searches.
I'm always a big advocate of this.

Not there's anything wrong with agencies listing themselves for sale, but if you go out and find companies off market, then, you know, as the buyer, then you're putting yourself in the driving seat of those conversations and you get much better deals.
And you usually find businesses that don't have a problem or as many problems they don't have, the founder looking to leave, etc.
So it can be a better situation to try as well if you're serious about making an acquisition so maybe we can send a bit more information over about that as well.
All right.
Well, thank you for the connection today.
And, yeah, let's stay in touch.
Yeah, Perfect.
All right.
Enjoy the rest of your day, Jason.
Enjoy some.
Thank you.
You as well.
Cheers.
See you soon.
Bye.
Thank you.
It.

**Andrew Day**
Double check if a majority of Lesley's business meets Jason's minimum client size requirements (19:47)
Discuss with Lesley whether she would be interested in having her book of business acquired rather than joining a larger firm (22:26)
Send information about Capital A's buy-side services to Jason (24:27)

**Jason Mudd**
Check back periodically with Capital A about potential acquisition targets (23:05)
summary.overview: In a recent Business Development and Acquisition Discussion meeting, Ahmed Zia of Capital A and Jason Mudd from Axia Public Relations explored a potential acquisition of Lesley Francis PR, which Capital A represents as it considers a retirement sale. The conversation began with personal introductions and transitioned into an examination of the compatibility between Axia's client base and Lesley’s, revealing concerns over the size of Lesley’s clients, which predominantly fall below Axia's acquisition threshold of $5,500/month in retainer fees. Both parties acknowledged that while Lesley's experience is significant, the opportunity may not be an ideal fit given Axia's primary interest in digital marketing agencies and client retention post-acquisition issues. Action items include Andrew verifying client size specifics and discussing alternative acquisition scenarios with Lesley, while Jason plans to maintain periodic communication regarding potential acquisition targets.
summary.short_summary: Ahmed Zia of Capital A and Jason Mudd from Axia Public Relations engaged in a discussion about the potential acquisition of Lesley Francis PR, which is considering a retirement sale. The meeting began with personal introductions and progressed to evaluating the compatibility of their client bases. Jason expressed concerns regarding the size of Lesley's clients, noting that most fall below Axia's minimum acquisition threshold of $5,500/month in retainer fees. They acknowledged Lesley’s significant experience but concluded that the opportunity might not be the right fit, particularly since Axia is primarily interested in digital marketing agencies and client retention issues post-acquisition. Action items included Andrew verifying specific client sizes and discussing alternative scenarios with Lesley, while Jason planned to keep communication open regarding future acquisition targets.
